image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Horizontal stacked bar chart.

2. **Layout techniques**:
- Uses **stacking** to show category shares within each student group.
- Uses **small multiples by row/category** only in the sense of separate horizontal bars for each student group.
- No faceting into separate panels.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Student group (traditional-aged undergraduates, adult undergraduates, graduate students) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; row labels |
| Expected class format category (Fully on-campus, little or no online; Majority on-campus, some online; A balance of campus/online; Majority online, some on-campus; Fully online) | Categorical/ordinal | Stacked segment order within each bar; color/hue; text headers above segments |
| Percentage / share of officers | Quantitative | Segment length/width along the x-axis; numeric labels inside segments |

Visible text elements:
- Title and subtitle provide context, but they are not additional plotted data variables.

I notice that more graduate students take online courses full-time when compared to other college levels, but most of the data for all college students was centered around a mix of both online and on-campus.  The data mimics that of a normal distribution which is surprising to me because I would think since COVID and the adaptations we had to do for online learning would sway the data that way.

Personally speaking, I wouldn’t be able to work full-time and travel to the campus and I’m only taking one course.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that for traditional-aged undergraduates it is expected for them to experience their classes majority on campus, some online. On the other hand, adult undergraduates are expected to experience their classes with a balance of campus/online. 

What do you wonder?
	For adult undergraduates, the majority online/some on campus is 32. For graduate students, the majority online/some on campus is 34. This is significantly higher than for traditional-aged undergraduates. I wonder if this is a result of the responsibilities that come at different ages. Traditional-aged undergraduates attend college immediately after graduating high school. Adult undergraduates may have taken some time off after high school or they have other responsibilities so it is more beneficial for them to experience a balance between campus and online. While traditional-aged undergraduates might have more time on their hands and campus classes are what they want. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me because I am a high school student and I graduate in 2024 so it is good to know what classes will look like for an undergraduate student. Some people may have thought that after the pandemic online classes would be over but they are still an option.  I think it is good that there is an online option for those who prefer that over on-campus classes.  

What’s going on in this graph?
The Normal in 2025: Online College

comments.raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the majority of the collected data prefer a hybrid schedule while a small amount wanted fully on-campus, with little, or no online. That's stating the obvious, but in a visual explanation, there's a skew seen in 4 out of the 5 categories for how students would like to do college. 

2. I understand why traditional-aged undergraduates would want classes in person because of the college experience. I wonder, though, are graduate students aiming for hybrid/online classes because they already experienced the typical "college life"? 

3. This relates to me in the sense that as a high school senior, when I applied for college, I aimed for classes that will take place in person as an undergraduate. I will soon fall under the traditional-aged undergraduate and be within the 4-44%. After the events of Covid-19 transitioning education to being taught online, several became used to it. With platforms like Zoom, it was obvious that their usage of them will grow even after the Covid-19 lockdown. By 2025, I'll be in my second year of college, so who knows what college would REALLY look like 2 years from now. All in the stats.

What I notice in this graph is that it is especially rare for college students to be completely in-person or completely online. On all three levels of higher education, it is more common to have online and in-person time split up. Young undergraduates are more likely than the other groups to be completely online, but only by 2-3%. Graduate students, on the other hand, have a significantly higher rate of fully online students compared to the other two groups. 

I am curious why graduate students have such a significantly higher rate of online students. This also makes me curious whether employers think degrees achieved online are less credible or valuable. I also wonder how largely this relates to the growing wage gap. Are more people going online because it is more affordable?

This relates to me and my community because after experiencing the pandemic, I know college students who still experience online class even though they live on campus. I am also going to college soon and had to decide whether I wanted to participate in an online university.

A title for this graph is: "Online Alternatives Sweep the Nation"

This relates to my community as I am starting college in the fall of 2023. This means I will be graduating college in 2027. It seems that it is highly likely I will have some online classes.

I noticed that most traditionally-aged undergraduates prefer to be mostly on campus while both adult undergraduates and graduates either prefer a balance of campus and online instruction or a majority of it to be online instruction. I wonder if graduate students prefer online instruction over in-person instruction as a result of being older and having to deal with more responsibilities, or if it’s due to something else. How does this relate to you and your community?

What do I notice?
According to these officers, a very small percentage of students, regardless of level, will be fully on-campus. The highest percentage for fully on-campus was 4% for traditional-aged undergraduates, a very small number. 
There also appears to be a statistically significant difference between the projected percentages for the different types of students, suggesting that there is an association between the type of student (traditional-aged undergraduates, adult undergraduates, and graduate students) and how the student is expected to experience college.

Potentially, this could be because traditional-aged undergraduates do not, generally, have full-time jobs and other outside commitments that would prevent them from attending school physically. 
I also notice that this study is limited by nonresponse bias, as only 271 responses were received from a total attempted sample of 4,700, and these people, who were willing to respond, likely have stronger or differing opinions from those who did not respond.

comments.raw_comment: This graph demonstrates the possible appearance of college classes in the near future.  There is an interesting array of future possible experiences.  The main thing that sticks out is how the traditional-aged undergraduates have the highest percentage for mostly on-campus instruction.  For this group, only 9% have majority online with a mere 2% fully online.  With the adult undergraduate section the online instruction percentages greatly increase to 32% for majority and 9% for fully.  Graduate students have the lowest in-person projected instruction with the highest online percentages of 34% majority and 17% fully.  This showcases how it is more likely for graduate students to take online courses.  The main thing I wonder is if it is necessarily easier for graduate students to take online courses.  I also wonder what this graph would have looked like before the pandemic forced schools to go virtual.  Did the pandemic prove that online instruction is easier than one would think?  This affects my community and I because almost all students across the nation have experienced online classes so it is necessary to understand whether or not that will be the case in college.  I would entitle this graph: "Future of College Classes."

- The largest number of prospective students who would go majority on-campus are traditional-aged undergraduates.

1.For tradition-aged undergraduates, the highest percentage lied in the section of Majority on-campus some online. For adult undergraduates, A balance of campus/online was the most frequent educational style. For graduate students, Majority online some on-campus classes were the most used. A pattern is seen where undergraduates prefer in person classes but then as they further their education, transition to online classes. To further this claim, only 2-9% of undergraduates are fully online whereas 17% of graduates are fully online. I also noticed is that not a lot of students are fully on campus: only 1-4% of undergraduates and graduates are fully online. 
2. What advantages can students find in choosing online courses over traditional ones? Do particular majors and courses encourage online work among their students?
3. This relates to me and my community as I have experienced online courses for two years for my first two years of high school as well as one month of online courses my junior year due to a surge of cases of the virus. I feel that online courses had a toll on my mental health as I was stuck in the same room for months on end. I also felt burdened with large amounts of work that my teachers expected to be done by the end of the day. I barely found any time for myself because I was so absorbed in my assignments.

1) What do you notice?
I notice that traditional undergraduate students prefer physical classrooms with little to no online course while nontraditional students tend to prefer online courses only. However, it is noticed that more commonly, students prefer to have a balance of both on-campus and online learning.

Many students have formed opinions on virtual learning and whether they prefer it over physical learning. If our school gave us the option to choose just as colleges are doing, our graphs would also fluctuate as there are many students who prefer one way of learning over the other. This graph also pertains to me since I will be entering college next year  and I may be presented with the decision of learning remotely or in person.
